questions.enonce_markdown:
Discuss the usefulness of the following in ICT:

(a) Legislation. (2 marks)

(b) Ergonomics. (2 marks)

(a) Differentiate between procedural programing and non-procedural programming. (2 marks)

(b) Name one procedural programming language and one non-procedural programming language. (2 marks)

(c) Describe three main features of an object oriented programming language. (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Procedural and non-procedural programming (2 marks).**

- In **procedural** programming the programmer writes, step by step and in order, *how* the computer must solve the problem, using sequences of instructions grouped in procedures or functions, with variables, decisions and loops.
- In **non-procedural** (declarative) programming the programmer states *what* result is wanted, or the facts and rules of the problem, and the language itself works out how to obtain it.

**(b) Examples (2 marks).** Procedural: C, Pascal, BASIC or FORTRAN. Non-procedural: SQL, Prolog (or a functional language such as Haskell).

**(c) Three main features of an object-oriented language (1 mark).**

- *Encapsulation:* the data (attributes) and the methods that work on them are bundled together in a class, and the data can be hidden from the outside.
- *Inheritance:* a new class takes over the attributes and methods of an existing class and adds its own, which allows code to be reused.
- *Polymorphism:* the same method name can behave differently according to the object that receives it. (Abstraction and the use of classes and objects are also accepted.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Identify and describe any four threats to data security. (2 marks)

(b) Define the term encryption and give its relevance. (3 marks)

(c) State two good password policies. (2 marks)

(d) Give two ways that may affect the integrity of data stored in the computer. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Four threats to data security (2 marks)** (any four):

- *Hacking (unauthorised access):* a person breaks into the system to read, change or steal data.
- *Malware (viruses, worms, ransomware, spyware):* harmful programs that corrupt, delete, lock or spy on data.
- *Phishing and social engineering:* fake e-mails, sites or calls that trick users into giving passwords or bank details.
- *Theft or loss of computers, disks and flash drives*, together with the data they hold.
- *Human error and dishonest staff:* accidental deletion, or an employee who copies or sells confidential data.
- *Hardware failure and disasters:* disk crash, power surge, fire or flood destroy the data if there is no backup.

**(b) Encryption (3 marks).** Encryption is the conversion of data (plain text) into an unreadable form (cipher text) by an algorithm and a secret key, so that only the person who has the right key can decrypt it back to plain text. *Relevance:* it protects the confidentiality of data stored on a disk and sent over a network (online banking, mobile money, e-mail, e-commerce): even when the data are intercepted or the device is stolen they cannot be understood, so privacy is kept and users have confidence in electronic services.

**(c) Two good password policies (2 marks)** (any two): a minimum length (at least 8 characters) mixing upper- and lower-case letters, digits and symbols; no personal information or dictionary words; changing passwords regularly and never re-using old ones; never sharing or writing down a password; locking the account after several failed attempts; two-factor authentication.

**(d) Two ways the integrity of stored data may be affected (2 marks)** (any two): human errors when entering or editing data; viruses or other malware, or unauthorised changes by hackers, which alter or corrupt the data; hardware faults or a power cut while data are being written; errors in the software; and transmission errors when data are copied or sent.
